finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL with axios. The only check is that the string starts with "https://". There is no host or IP allowlist, no check on resolved addresses, and no limit on redirects. A client can make the server request internal HTTPS hosts, any port, or an attacker-controlled HTTPS host that 302-redirects to http://169.254.169.254/... or http://users.internal:8080/.... axios follows redirects by default (maxRedirects=5) and does not restrict the scheme on redirect, so the https-only check is bypassed. Hostnames that resolve to private IPs, and DNS rebinding, also pass. The response body is not returned (only its byte length), so this is semi-blind. It still gives a reachability, size and error oracle, and can trigger side-effecting GET requests against internal services.

trace.note: only validation: typeof string and startsWith("https://"). No host, IP or port restriction.
axios.get(url) with default redirect following, so a redirect can reach http:// internal targets
response reveals img.data.length. Errors (unhandled rejection or 500) give a connect/TLS/timeout oracle.

finding.guards_checked: The prefix check url.startsWith("https://") is a scheme check on the original string only. It is not a host check, and it is not applied to redirect targets. There is no DNS resolution or IP check, no allowlist, no maxRedirects:0 and no egress proxy. The only other guard is the typeof string check. No parser is used for validation, so there is no parser differential to bypass. The gap is that nothing is validated.

verdict.guard_found: none (only typeof string and startsWith("https://") scheme-prefix check at server.js:11; no auth middleware, no host allowlist, no redirect limit)
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl from an unauthenticated route, server.js:11 only checks the "https://" prefix, and server.js:14 calls axios.get(url) with default redirects and no host validation, so SSRF is reachable.
